beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on routing and determinism: how the physics engine makes sure the same problem always gets the same answer. The team ran one problem ten times, and compared every byte of the output. All ten were identical. Here's why that isn't luck.

props.command: How does the physics engine guarantee the same problem always gets the same answer?
output: SymPy has no randomness in it
Variation can only come from formula choice or a model
So the route is decided before solving

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, why the solver can't disagree with itself. Second, the only two places variation can sneak in. And third, the three routes the engine chooses between, and why it chooses before solving anything. No physics or coding background needed.

beats.new_visual_element: the solver can't be the cause
beats.narration_text: The answer up front. SymPy has no randomness in it. Same equations, same numbers, same answer, every time. So if the same problem ever gets two different answers, the solver isn't the cause. It's either which formula got picked, or a language model sampling differently. The engine checks the first one before solving, and labels every answer with its route.

So there are only two places variation can come from. One: formula selection. If two cards could both answer the question, and nothing chooses between them, the result depends on which one happens to come first. Two: a language model doing part of the work, and sampling differently from run to run. Running the problem twice won't catch the first one. SymPy can't disagree with itself.

So before solving, the engine counts how many cards can actually close. Exactly one, and the route is called deterministic script: the answer is final. Zero, and there's no deterministic path: a model or a human handles it, and the gap is logged. More than one, and it's ambiguous. Every candidate answer comes back, and a model is asked only to choose which formula applies, never to redo the math.

beats.new_visual_element: thirty, or two point three seven
beats.narration_text: The team built a case to prove it. The knowns describe both a car speeding up, and a compressed spring. Both cards close on the same unknown: speed. One says thirty meters per second. The other says about two point three seven. A system that silently took the first card would look perfectly consistent, and could be confidently wrong. The engine reports both, and asks.

Why defend determinism this hard? Three reasons, from the team's own notes. Grading fairness: two students with the same problem must be graded against the same reference. Debuggability: a wrong answer that comes with its route and its matched card tells you exactly what to fix. And cost: a symbolic solve is cheaper and faster than calling a language model by default.

beats.new_visual_element: what the ten runs do and don't prove
beats.narration_text: Now the limit. The ten identical runs prove the solver, after the problem has been read. Reading still uses a language model, and newer Claude models don't take a randomness setting, so that step can vary. And the team asks the hard question about its own design: is routing the right call, or just a way of avoiding hard problems?

So here's the takeaway. Consistency you can explain beats consistency you hope for. When an A.I. model gives you an answer, ask which method it chose, and why. If the method can change, so can the answer.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any problem that could be solved more than one way. It asks Claude to list the methods before picking one.

props.command: Here is a problem: [paste it]. Before solving, list every formula or method that could apply, and what each one assumes. If more than one fits, solve with each, compare the answers, and explain which one actually matches the situation.
output: The one that fits, and why
